factual_claims.text: A white stork was found in 1822 near Klutz in Mecklenburg, Germany, with a spear lodged through its neck.
The spear was about 75 cm long and came from central Africa, where the bird had been wintering.
Before migration was understood, naturalists held that storks and swallows hibernated underwater or changed into other animals.
Because the spear was identified as central African, the stork must have been wounded there and flown back to Germany.
The stuffed stork is kept in the zoological collection of the University of Rostock, and about 25 Pfeilstorche had been documented in Germany as of 2003.

segments.narration: A stork landed in Germany with a spear through it. The bird was alive, nesting, behaving as if nothing had happened.
Mecklenburg, 1822. The shaft ran two and a half feet long, and no hunter in Europe carried a weapon anything like it.
So where had the bird been? Every winter Europe's storks vanished. Naturalists argued they hibernated underwater, or changed into other creatures entirely.
The spear was identified as central African. That meant the stork had been speared there, survived it, and flown thousands of miles home.
One bird proved migration. It is still in Rostock's collection, stuffed, spear included, and roughly two dozen more have turned up since.

research.summary: The Rostocker Pfeilstorch is a white stork found in 1822 near Klutz, then in the Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, alive with a 75 cm central African spear lodged in its neck. Until then the winter disappearance of storks and swallows was explained by underwater hibernation or transmutation into other animals, ideas promoted by zoologists of the period. The spear's central African origin showed the bird had wintered there and flown back, which is the physical evidence for long-distance migration. The stuffed specimen is held in the zoological collection of the University of Rostock; about 25 Pfeilstorche had been documented in Germany as of 2003, and later cases include a stork from Tanganyika and a honey buzzard from Finland. Audubon's account credits the examination to Heinrich Gustav Florke and places the wound in the Upper Nile region.

segments.narration: Oak Island has swallowed 230 years of treasure hunting. Nova Scotia, 1795: a dip in the ground and three teenagers with shovels.
Ten feet down, flagstones. Below that, oak platforms every ten feet, all the way to ninety. Then the shaft flooded and the digging stopped.
Every generation since has tried again. Pumps, drills, a causeway built in 1965 just to haul heavy machinery across. Nothing.
So what is actually down there? Geologists point at the bedrock: limestone and gypsum, the rock that dissolves into caves and then caves in.
In 1878 a farmer's oxen crashed through the ground 120 yards away, into a natural cavern. The money pit was probably a sinkhole all along.

research.summary: Oak Island, Nova Scotia, has been dug for treasure since an often-retold 1795 account of local youth Daniel McInnis noticing a depression. Early companies reported oak platforms down to about ninety feet before flooding stopped work; a causeway was built in 1965 for heavy machinery. Nothing of value has ever been confirmed. The island is a composite of four drumlins with Windsor Group limestone and gypsum bedrock, and skeptics including Joe Nickell and Brian Dunning argue the pit is a natural sinkhole — a reading supported by an 1878 incident in which a ploughing farmer's oxen broke through into a natural cavern about 120 yards from the pit.

segments.narration: A wooden machine beat Napoleon at chess in 1809. Schonbrunn Palace, Vienna: a life-size figure in robes, bolted to a cabinet of gears.
Wolfgang von Kempelen built it in 1770 for Empress Maria Theresa. Before each game he opened the cabinet doors to prove nothing was inside.
It played Benjamin Franklin. It toured London, Leipzig, Havana, Baltimore. Eighty-four years on the road, mostly winning.
So how does a box of cogs read a chessboard? Edgar Allan Poe published his theory in 1836 and got most of it wrong.
A man was folded inside on a sliding seat, reading moves off magnets under each square. In 1827 the operator fainted in Baltimore and two boys watched him climb out.

research.summary: Wolfgang von Kempelen's chess-playing automaton was working by 1769, completed in early 1770, and debuted at Schonbrunn Palace before Empress Maria Theresa. It was exhibited for 84 years, touring France, London, Leipzig and Dresden under Kempelen and later Britain, the United States and Havana under Johann Nepomuk Maelzel. It beat Napoleon Bonaparte at Schonbrunn in 1809 after 19 moves, played Benjamin Franklin in Paris, and lost to Philidor. The machine was not automatic: a human chess player sat concealed in the cabinet on a sliding seat that let him shift as the doors were opened, reading each move from magnets suspended under the 64 numbered squares, with dummy machinery sliding into place to hide him. In 1827 operator William Schlumberger fainted from the heat in Baltimore and two boys saw him leave the cabinet; the Baltimore Gazette reported it on 1 June 1827 and few believed it. The Turk burned on 5 July 1854 in Philadelphia, and Silas Mitchell published the first full explanation in The Chess Monthly in 1857.

segments.narration: One image on 4chan started a fourteen-year treasure hunt. January 4th, 2012. White text on a black square.
Data was hidden inside the picture. Then a phone number. Then websites, ciphers, and paper signs with QR codes taped up in cities worldwide.
The clues quoted Welsh myth, cyberpunk poetry, occult texts. Every one of them was signed with the same PGP key.
Who runs a global cipher hunt and never asks for money? New rounds opened in 2013 and 2014. Then came a runic book nobody can finish.

The most credible answer is the boring one: recruitment. Solvers who got through were invited to a private forum and handed a project. The last signed message arrived in April 2017. Nobody has proved who sent it.

research.summary: Cicada 3301 posted its first puzzle on 4chan on 4 January 2012; it ran for close to a month. Clues covered cryptography, steganography and internet anonymity and included images with hidden data, a telephone message, websites and paper signs carrying QR codes, alongside references to the Mabinogion, the poem Agrippa and The Book of the Law. Further rounds began on 4 January 2013 and 4 January 2014, the latter posted on Twitter and still unsolved; a further clue appeared in January 2016. Every clue was signed with the same OpenPGP private key, and the last confirmed communication was an OpenPGP-signed message in April 2017 disavowing unsigned puzzles. The runic Liber Primus remains largely undeciphered. Theories about the group range from intelligence-agency recruitment to a cyber-mercenary group, an alternate reality game, or a privacy-focused secret society; the group said it was seeking highly intelligent individuals, and solvers who passed were invited to a private forum and given a project. Its identity and ultimate purpose are unknown.

A Woods Hole team first caught it on US Navy listening arrays, hardware built to track submarines and opened to scientists in 1992.
It has turned up every year since. Aleutians down to California, August through December. One voice, off-key, never answered.
So who is it calling? The pitch has crept down to about fifty hertz, which is just what an animal growing older sounds like.

research.summary: A Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution team first detected a 52-hertz whale call in 1989, and again in 1990 and 1991; in 1992 the US Navy partially declassified its SOSUS hydrophone arrays and made them available for oceanographic research. The call sits at 52 Hz, well above blue whales (10-39 Hz) and fin whales (about 20 Hz), and is shorter and more frequent than theirs. It has been detected every year since, tracking from the Aleutian and Kodiak Islands south to the California coast between August and December; a 2004 study covered twelve years of tracking and noted the call had deepened to around 50 Hz, consistent with maturation. The animal has never been seen. Scientists suggest it is malformed or a blue-fin hybrid; a 2021 documentary included footage of a blue-fin hybrid believed to be the source, and marine biologist John Calambokidis has argued for a part-blue, part-fin animal. Calls picked up by a California sensor in 2010 suggest more than one whale calls at this frequency.

research.summary: Project Iceworm was a classified US Army Cold War plan for mobile nuclear missile launch sites under the Greenland ice sheet, using a tunnel network of about 4,000 km to deploy up to 600 missiles with launch clusters four miles apart. Its cover was Camp Century, launched in 1959 in northwestern Greenland at about 2,000 m elevation and roughly 240 km from Thule Air Base, powered from 1960 to 1963 by the Alco-designed PM-2A portable reactor. Denmark approved Camp Century but never gave consent for missile deployment. The ice sheet deformed the tunnels: by mid-1962 the reactor room ceiling had dropped and had to be raised five feet, and ice cores showed the glacier moving faster than expected. The facility was evacuated in 1965, the camp closed in 1966, and the project was cancelled. Details surfaced from January 1995 during a Danish Foreign Policy Institute inquiry. A 2016 study by Colgan et al. in Geophysical Research Letters found the ice over Camp Century could start to melt by 2100 on current trends, which would risk remobilising buried waste including about 200,000 litres of diesel, PCBs and radioactive waste.

It is undeciphered because the inscriptions are too short, no bilingual or digraphic text has been found, the Harappan language is unidentified, and no Indus rulers or personal names are attested elsewhere. Rao), Munda, and a non-linguistic reading argued by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel in 2004 and disputed by Parpola and Rao et al. in 2009. In January 2025 Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M. K. Stalin announced a US$1 million prize for a decipherment.

segments.narration: A thousand American soldiers fought the war with inflatable tanks. The 23rd Headquarters Special Troops. Activated January 1944. Their job was to be seen.

research.summary: The 23rd Headquarters Special Troops, nicknamed the Ghost Army, was a US tactical deception unit of roughly 1,100 men (82 officers and 1,023 enlisted in some accounts) activated 20 January 1944 and modelled on British deception at El Alamein. The unit worked near Normandy, Brest, Luxembourg, the Hurtgen Forest and a major Rhine crossing, in more than 20 deception campaigns, returning to the US in July 1945. The operation stayed classified until 1996. President Biden signed the Ghost Army Congressional Gold Medal Act on 1 February 2022 and the medal was presented at the US Capitol on 21 March 2024.

February 1864, off Charleston. The Hunley drove a spar torpedo into the USS Housatonic, sinking it in three minutes. History's first submarine kill.
Then it never came home. Twenty-one men died inside this boat across three separate sinkings. So what killed the final eight?
Located in 1995, raised in 2000. No skeleton showed injury. The pump was never set to clear water. Nobody had released the escape weights.

research.summary: The Confederate submarine H. L. Hunley sank three times, killing 21 men in all: five on 29 August 1863, eight on 15 October 1863 including Horace Hunley, and eight on 17 February 1864 after it drove a spar torpedo into the 1,240-ton USS Housatonic off Charleston, sinking it in about three minutes with five of her crew lost. Diver Ralph Wilbanks located the wreck in April 1995 on a NUMA expedition and it was raised on 8 August 2000. The remains were found seated at their stations with no skeletal trauma and no sign of an escape attempt; in 2008 researchers reported the bilge pump had not been set to clear the crew compartment, and in 2018 that the keel release blocks had never been released. A 2017 PLOS ONE study by Duke blast-trauma researchers led by Rachel Lance concluded the crew were most likely killed instantly by pulmonary blast trauma from their own 135-pound black-powder torpedo, detonated less than 16 feet from the bow, with individual survival odds under about 16 per cent. Naval History and Heritage Command archaeologists have disputed that conclusion.

research.summary: The Stone of Scone, about 336 lb (152 kg), was used in the coronation of Scottish monarchs until Edward I seized it in 1296 and had it built into a chair at Westminster Abbey, after which English and British monarchs were crowned over it. On Christmas Day 1950 four Scottish students — Ian Hamilton, Kay Matheson, Gavin Vernon and Alan Stuart — removed it from the Abbey; it broke into two pieces during the removal. The larger part was buried in a field in Kent, then taken to Scotland and left on the altar of Arbroath Abbey, where it was recovered on 11 April 1951 and returned to Westminster about four months after the theft. The four were identified but no charges were brought; secondary accounts attribute this to a decision not to inflame Scottish nationalism. The UK government announced the stone's return to Scotland on 3 July 1996; it moved to Edinburgh Castle on 15 November 1996 with the official handover on St Andrew's Day, 30 November 1996. It remains Crown property and is taken to London for coronations, and since March 2024 it has been on permanent display at Perth Museum. The Westminster Stone theory holds that monks hid the real stone in 1296 and the English took a substitute.

research.summary: On 27 November 1810 the occupant of 54 Berners Street, Westminster — a Mrs Tottenham (sometimes spelled Tottingham) — was buried in uninvited callers and deliveries. Chimney sweeps arrived at 5 a.m., followed by dozens of coal wagons from the Paddington wharves, about a dozen bakers with wedding cakes, furniture, organs and a coffin; police blocked both ends of the street and a final wave of domestic servants expecting job interviews arrived at 5 p.m. Among the dignitaries drawn there were the Duke of Gloucester and the chairmen of the Bank of England and the East India Company; the Lord Mayor went on to the Marlborough Street magistrates to have police sent. The hoax was arranged by Theodore Hook, then 22, who had planned it from October 1810 with two accomplices and sent somewhere between one thousand and four thousand letters in Mrs Tottenham's name, for a one-guinea wager that he could make the address the most talked-about in London. A reward was offered and nobody was charged; Hook was suspected by 1812 and effectively confessed in his 1835 novel Gilbert Gurney.
